title: Parallelism

objectives.can: Divide a verse of poetry into its lines and describe how the second line answers the first.

explanation.summary: Hebrew poetry is built from short lines, and the sense of a verse usually runs across two or three of them: the second line answers the first. Learning to see the lines, and to ask what each later line adds, is the first skill of reading the Psalms and the prophets.

sections.heading: Lines, not rhymes
body: A verse of Hebrew poetry is usually made of two short lines, sometimes three. Each line is called a colon (plural cola). The lines are not set apart by rhyme, and the library's texts print them as running text, so the reader must find the break.

Scholars have long tried to describe the rhythm of the lines, often by counting stressed words, and they still disagree about how far Hebrew poetry has a fixed metre. This lesson does not depend on that question. It looks at the meaning: how the second line stands to the first.

sections.heading: Where the verse divides: the atnah
body: The accent called atnah (a small sign under the stressed syllable of one word) marks the main pause inside a verse. In a two-line verse it usually stands on the last word of the first line, and the silluq (the sign under the last word, just before the two dots that close the verse) marks the end of the second line. In Psalm 1:6 the atnah stands under צַדִּיקִים: the first line is 'the LORD knows the way of the righteous', and the second line follows it.

The atnah does not always cut the verse into two equal halves. In Psalm 1:1 there are three lines, and the atnah stands on עָמַד, at the end of the second line. In Psalm 1:3 it stands at the end of the second line of three. The accents are an old tradition about how to phrase the verse: they usually agree with the lines, but a reader still uses the sense to decide.

sections.heading: Lowth's three kinds
body: In 1753 Robert Lowth described the relation between lines as synonymous, antithetic or synthetic. His names are still the classical description, and they are a useful first sorting.

Later scholars, such as James Kugel and Robert Alter, have shown that the second line rarely just repeats the first. It usually sharpens the first line, makes it more specific or carries the thought forward: 'A, and what is more, B.' So treat Lowth's names as a starting point and always ask what the second line adds.

head: Kind
What the second line does
Where to look
rows: Says the same thing in other words, usually with something added
Sets a contrast, often the righteous against the wicked
Completes or builds on the first line, with no close echo

sections.heading: Asking what the second line adds
body: When you have found two lines, ask three questions. Which words answer each other? What does the second line say that the first did not? Is a word left out of the second line because the first line supplies it?

The answering words are often a word pair: two words that Hebrew poets set side by side, such as 'day' and 'night' or 'heavens' and 'expanse'. The second word of the pair is seldom an exact synonym. It may be more specific, or it may name the other half of a whole. The word left out is usually the verb: a verb in the first line does duty for both lines. Psalm 1:5 is an example, and you will meet more in the next lesson.

head: Pair
Where
How the second word relates
rows: The two halves of a whole: all the time
The heavens, then the expanse of the sky
Two names for the same group; the second is more specific

sections.heading: Verse numbers in the Psalms
body: The edition numbers the Psalms as the Hebrew text does, and a heading belongs to verse 1. Psalm 19 has a heading, so its first line of poetry is verse 2, and the verses called 8 to 10 in this lesson are numbered 7 to 9 in many English Bibles. Psalm 1 has no heading.

misunderstandings: The second line is not a mere repetition. Look for what it adds: a more specific word, a new idea, a time, an effect.
The atnah is not a comma and does not mark two equal halves. It is a traditional sign of the main pause, and it can fall after the second of three lines.
Lowth's three kinds are not sealed boxes. Many verses show two of them at once, and some fit none well.
Words in a word pair are not exact synonyms. רְשָׁעִים and חַטָּאִים both name the wrongdoer, but each brings its own shade.

deeper.heading: Counting stresses
body: Gray, in a classic study of the forms of Hebrew poetry, described the lines by counting their stressed beats. Many scholars still find a rough balance between lines, but there is no agreed theory that explains every line, and some Psalms are hard to scan. A beginner is on safe ground with the meaning-based method of this lesson.

deeper.heading: Word pairs in neighbouring languages
body: Scholars have noticed that some Hebrew word pairs also appear in the poetry of neighbouring peoples, for example in the Ugaritic texts. This suggests that the pairs belong to a shared poetic craft, but it does not tell us what any one pair means in a given verse; only the verse itself does.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament showeth His handiwork;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two lines, divided by the atnah on אֵל. Line one: 'the heavens are telling the glory of God'. Line two: 'and the work of his hands the expanse proclaims'. The pair הַשָּׁמַיִם // הָרָקִיעַ answers itself, and the participles מְסַפְּרִים // מַגִּיד answer each other. The second line is not a bare repeat: 'glory' becomes the concrete 'work of his hands', and the word order is turned about (object, then verb, then subject). Lowth would call this synonymous.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night revealeth knowledge;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Day answers night, and the two verbs answer each other, as יַבִּיעַ // יְחַוֶּה. The atnah on אֹמֶר divides the verse. 'Day to day pours out speech, and night to night declares knowledge.' The second line adds something: 'speech' becomes 'knowledge'. The pair יוֹם // לַיְלָה names the whole of time, so the message goes on without a break.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: For the LORD regardeth the way of the righteous; but the way of the wicked shall perish.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: An antithetic verse. The atnah on צַדִּיקִים ends the first line: 'the LORD knows the way of the righteous'. The second line, 'but the way of the wicked will perish', turns the thought round. It does not simply deny the first; it says that the way itself, and not only the person, comes to nothing. The same word דֶּרֶךְ stands in both lines, and the pair צַדִּיקִים // רְשָׁעִים gives the contrast.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: BOOK I HAPPY IS the man that hath not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of the scornful.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three lines, each with a negative and a verb: הָלַךְ, עָמַד, יָשַׁב. The atnah stands on עָמָד, at the end of the second line, and the third line stands alone after it. The nouns also step along: בַּעֲצַת רְשָׁעִים, בְּדֶרֶךְ חַטָּאִים, וּבְמוֹשַׁב לֵצִים. Many readers see the three verbs as a growing settledness: walking, standing, sitting. The three lines are one thought told three times, with a new shade each time.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: And he shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, that bringeth forth its fruit in its season, and whose leaf doth not wither; and in whatsoever he doeth he shall prosper.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A synthetic verse. The first line gives the picture: a tree planted by streams of water. The second gives what the tree does: its fruit in its season, its leaf does not wither. The atnah on יִבּוֹל closes these two. The third line, וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה יַצְלִיחַ, leaves the picture and says what it means for the man's work: whatever he does succeeds.

practice.prompt: How does the second line of this verse (from כִּי אִם) stand to the first?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Not so the wicked; but they are like the chaff which the wind driveth away.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It sets the wicked against the picture of the righteous: not so, but like chaff
It asks a question about the first line
It repeats the first line in other words
practice.explain: The first line says that the wicked are not like the tree of the verse before. The second line, with כִּי אִם, 'but rather', gives the contrasting picture: chaff driven by the wind. The relation is a contrast, not a repeat.

practice.prompt: The second line (וְחַטָּאִים בַּעֲדַת צַדִּיקִים) has no verb. Which word from the first line is understood in it?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Therefore the wicked shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: The verb יָקֻמוּ, 'will stand', and the negative לֹא serve both lines: 'the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the company of the righteous'. The second line is shorter because the first line supplies its verb.

practice.prompt: The second line repeats the idea of 'his delight is in the law of the LORD'. What does it add?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in His law doth he meditate day and night.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The manner and the time: he meditates on it day and night
practice.explain: וּבְתוֹרָתוֹ answers בְּתוֹרַת יְהוָה, and the verb יֶהְגֶּה, 'he murmurs, he meditates', answers חֶפְצוֹ, 'his delight'. The second line then adds יוֹמָם וָלָיְלָה, 'by day and by night'. It is not a bare echo.

practice.prompt: In the first line of this verse the poet writes הַשָּׁמַיִם. Which word answers it in the second line?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament showeth His handiwork;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: הָרָקִיעַ, 'the expanse', is the word that answers 'the heavens'. מַגִּיד answers the participle of line one, not the subject, and יָדָיו answers אֵל.

practice.prompt: In the line that begins יוֹם לְיוֹם, which word is the partner of יוֹם in the second line?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night revealeth knowledge;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: Day and night are the two halves of a whole, and the pair means 'all the time'. דַּעַת answers אֹמֶר, and יְחַוֶּה answers יַבִּיעַ.

quoted.english: For forty years was I wearied with that generation, and said: It is a people that do err in their heart, and they have not known My ways;

quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: הַ֝מֵּבִ֗ין is Hiphil, participle (active), participle, masculine, singular, absolute, from בִּין (discern, perceive).

check.prompt: This verse has three lines. On which word does the atnah stand, closing the second line?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: BOOK I HAPPY IS the man that hath not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of the scornful.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: The atnah stands on עָמָד, which ends the line 'and in the way of sinners has not stood'. The third line, 'and in the seat of the scornful has not sat', is closed by the silluq at the end of the verse. The atnah does not always fall in the middle.

check.prompt: How does the second line of this verse stand to the first?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: For the LORD regardeth the way of the righteous; but the way of the wicked shall perish.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It says the same thing again with different words
It asks who the righteous are
It contrasts the way of the wicked with the way of the righteous
check.explain: The first line is about what the LORD knows of the way of the righteous. The second line, with דֶּרֶךְ again, turns to the way of the wicked, which will perish. The relation is a contrast (Lowth's antithetic), and the second line goes further than a plain opposite.

check.prompt: What do the three verbs הָלַךְ, עָמַד, יָשַׁב do across the three lines?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: BOOK I HAPPY IS the man that hath not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of the scornful.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: They repeat one action three times in the same sense
They change the time from past to future
They give three acts, often read as a step-by-step settling in: walking, standing, sitting
check.explain: All three are the same form and each is negated, but they name different acts. Many readers take the series as a growing settledness. That is a reading of the parallel lines, not a proof, but it fits a poet who avoids plain repetition.

check.prompt: The first line begins תּוֹרַת יְהוָה. Which word in the second line is its partner?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: The law of the LORD is perfect, restoring the soul; the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: תּוֹרַת יְהוָה // עֵדוּת יְהוָה: the same pattern, a noun in the construct state before the divine name. The two nouns name the same thing from slightly different sides, 'instruction' and 'testimony'. The word נֶפֶשׁ is paired with פֶּתִי across the two lines.

check.prompt: The last line (וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה יַצְלִיחַ) follows the atnah. What does it do?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: And he shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, that bringeth forth its fruit in its season, and whose leaf doth not wither; and in whatsoever he doeth he shall prosper.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It turns to the man's own work and says that whatever he does succeeds
It contrasts the tree with chaff
It repeats that the tree is planted by streams
It asks how long the tree will live
check.explain: The first two lines paint the tree. The third line leaves the picture and states the point of it for the man: success in what he does. This is the kind of verse Lowth called synthetic, where the later line builds on the earlier one.

check.prompt: The two lines of this verse are built alike: a noun, יְהוָה, an adjective, and a participle phrase. Which of Lowth's kinds fits best?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: The precepts of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Antithetic, because the second line denies the first
Synonymous, with a new effect in each line: the heart is gladdened, the eyes are lit
Synthetic, because the second line asks a question
None: the verse is not poetry
check.explain: פִּקּוּדֵי // מִצְוַת, יְשָׁרִים // בָּרָה, מְשַׂמְּחֵי־לֵב // מְאִירַת עֵינָיִם: each part answers the part before it, and the two effects differ. That is synonymous parallelism with a sharpening.

check.prompt: The second line of this verse is not a plain copy of the first. What does 'the work of his hands' do to 'the glory of God'?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament showeth His handiwork;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It makes it concrete: the glory is the visible handiwork of God
It changes the subject to the earth
check.explain: In the first line the heavens tell of 'glory', which is abstract. In the second the expanse proclaims 'the work of his hands', which is what the eye sees. The second line sharpens the first, which is typical.

check.prompt: In the pair of lines יוֹם לְיוֹם יַבִּיעַ אֹמֶר // וְלַיְלָה לְלַיְלָה יְחַוֶּה דָּעַת, what is new in the second line?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night revealeth knowledge;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'Speech' becomes 'knowledge': what is said is something known
check.explain: אֹמֶר is 'speech' or 'utterance'; דַּעַת is 'knowledge'. The second line takes the thought one step on. Both lines have their own verb, so nothing is left out.

reading.why: The whole of Psalm 1 has no heading. It shows a three-line verse (1:1), a verse with a long image (1:3), an antithetic pair of lines (1:4 and 1:6) and a verse that leaves a verb out of the second line (1:5). Read each verse by asking where the atnah falls and what each later line adds.
